summary: This Standards Track document specifies the architecture, signaling, and procedures for Point-to-Multipoint Policies in Segment Routing, for both SR-MPLS and SRv6. It defines the policy construct, its candidate paths, and the instantiation of P2MP tree instances for efficient multipoint delivery. It updates RFC 9524.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing the same letter many times, build one delivery tree that branches so each branch carries a copy toward its recipients.

questions: what is an sr p2mp policy
what is a p2mp tree instance
subtitle: How Segment Routing builds efficient multicast-style delivery trees from a policy, using Replication segments.

tldr.problem: A single Replication segment from the ingress to every egress gives ingress replication, which sends the same traffic over the same nodes and links again and again.
tldr.mechanism: An SR P2MP Policy names a Root and Leaf nodes and has candidate paths. A controller computes P2MP tree instances for them and installs Replication segments stitched together from the Root through intermediate Replication nodes to the Leaves.
tldr.outcome: Multipoint traffic is copied only where the tree branches, for both SR-MPLS and SRv6. The RFC also updates how the Replication-ID in RFC 9524 is structured.

today: RFC 9960 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2026. It updates RFC 9524, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: From Ingress Replication to Trees
sections.content:
RFC 9524 defines a Replication segment, which lets a Segment Routing (SR) node copy traffic to several downstream nodes. One Replication segment spanning from the ingress to all the egress nodes of a service would achieve ingress replication, which is inefficient because the traffic may cross the same nodes and links many times.

RFC 9960 instead builds a P2MP tree. It runs from a Root node to a set of Leaf nodes through intermediate Replication nodes. It consists of a Replication segment at the Root, stitched to Replication segments at the Leaves and the intermediate Replication nodes. A Bud node is both a Replication node and a Leaf.

The document specifies the architecture, signaling and procedures for SR P2MP Policies with SR over MPLS (SR-MPLS) and SR over IPv6 (SRv6), and the controller extensions needed to compute and provision them. It also updates the Replication-ID part of the Replication segment identifier defined in RFC 9524.
sections.eli5: Sending one copy to every friend by yourself is slow and repeats the same trip. A tree sends one copy down the main road and only splits it where the roads fork.

sections.title: Policies, Candidate Paths and Tree Instances
sections.content:
An SR P2MP Policy defines the Root and Leaf nodes of a tree and has one or more candidate paths (CPs), each optionally carrying constraints and optimization objectives. The policy is identified by the tuple <Root, Tree-ID>, where the Root is an IP address and the Tree-ID is a 32-bit unsigned integer.

A CP is identified by <Protocol-Origin, Originator, Discriminator> as in RFC 9256, and the Root selects the active CP using the tiebreaking rules in that RFC. A CP has zero or more P2MP tree instances (PTIs). It has none if the controller cannot compute a tree for it, and it can have more than one, for example during Make-Before-Break. One and only one PTI MUST be active for a CP, otherwise duplicate traffic may reach the Leaf nodes. A PTI is identified by an Instance-ID, an unsigned 16-bit number unique within the policy.

The update to RFC 9524 is that the Replication-ID becomes the tuple <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID>. A Replication segment of a PTI is then identified in the control plane by <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID, Node-ID>. The simple 32-bit case maps to a zero Root, a zero Instance-ID and the 32-bit Tree-ID. Each PTI has its own Replication segment and unique Replication-SID at a given node, because different trees need different replication state.

Explicit CPs with a static tree topology can also be provisioned using NETCONF/YANG or the CLI, but a static tree will not adapt to network changes.
sections.eli5: A policy is a plan for who the sender is and who must receive. A candidate path is one way you might do it, and a tree instance is the actual set of branches built for that plan right now.

sections.title: Steering Traffic into a Policy
sections.content:
The Replication-SID of the Replication segment at the Root is called the Tree-SID of a PTI. It is RECOMMENDED that the Tree-SID also be used as the Replication-SID at the intermediate Replication nodes and Leaf nodes, which simplifies operations and troubleshooting, although those nodes MAY use different values. For SRv6 the Replication-SID is the FUNCT portion of the SID, so the locator portion still differs between nodes.

Each policy has a Binding SID (BSID). It steers traffic when the Root is not the ingress node of the SR domain. The packet is steered to the Root with a segment list whose last segment is the BSID. The BSID SHOULD stay constant for the life of the policy, although it MAY be the Tree-SID of the active PTI, in which case it changes when the active CP or PTI changes.

The Root can steer an incoming packet in two ways:

  • Local-policy-based forwarding: the Root maps the packet to the active PTI of the active CP using local policy. How is out of scope.
  • Tree-SID-based forwarding: the BSID in the packet is replaced with the Tree-SID of the active PTI, and the packet is replicated to the downstream Replication-SIDs.

For SR-MPLS with local-policy forwarding, the Root SHOULD set the MPLS TTL so the copy can reach the furthest Leaf.
sections.eli5: The tree has a front door with a name tag. Traffic either gets sent to the door by its tag, or the first router just recognizes it and pushes it in.

sections.title: The P2MP Tree Instance
sections.content:
A PTI has a Replication segment at the Root, zero or more at intermediate Replication nodes, and one at each Leaf. When a packet enters, the Root replicates it and each copy carries the Replication-SID of the downstream node. A downstream node is either a Leaf, where replication ends, or an intermediate Replication node that replicates further. If a Replication node and its downstream node are not adjacent, SR-MPLS inserts one or more SIDs before the downstream Replication-SID, while SRv6 can use the locator of the downstream SID or an optional segment list.

At Leaf nodes the Tree-SID or Replication-SID is tied to the service context. In SR-MPLS, if services can be told apart by their service label, a controller MAY skip Replication segments at the Leaves and upstream nodes remove the Tree-SID. In SRv6 the Replication segments MUST be instantiated on the Leaves, because behavior like Penultimate Hop Popping is not feasible when the Tree-SID is in the IPv6 Destination Address.

A Replication segment MAY be shared across PTIs, for example for local protection of the adjacency between a Replication node X and a downstream node Y. A shared segment MUST use a zero Root, a zero Instance-ID and a Tree-ID unique on that node.
sections.eli5: At each fork a helper makes copies and hands one to each branch. When a copy reaches someone at the end of a branch, it stops being copied.

sections.title: Controller Procedures
sections.content:
The document focuses on a controller, such as a Path Computation Element (PCE), that computes and installs trees. It discovers topology across IGP areas, levels or ASes, and exchanges capabilities with nodes. A controller MUST compute a tree with no loops at steady state. It SHOULD change a PTI when the topology change affects it or a better path appears, and it MAY use Make-Before-Break: create the new PTI, activate it once instantiated, then remove the old one.

The controller assigns Replication-SIDs, either dynamically or as statically set by whoever provisions the policy. For SR-MPLS it is RECOMMENDED to take them from the SR Local Block (SRLB) and NOT RECOMMENDED to take them from the SR Global Block (SRGB), which is globally significant and can be depleted. The same advice, to use the SRLB, applies to the policy BSID.

The controller instantiates Replication segments with signaling such as PCEP, BGP or NETCONF/YANG. A node SHOULD report success or failure, and on failure the controller SHOULD retry up to an upper bound and then raise a rate-limited alert. It is RECOMMENDED to tear down the PTI if the Root's segment fails. One approach is to install Leaves and intermediate nodes first, then the Root.

For protection, backup SR Policies can protect a link, node or branch locally, and loop-free alternates or TI-LFA can also be used. A controller can provide path protection with a backup CP whose trees are disjoint from the active one.
sections.eli5: A planner draws the delivery map, tells each stop what to do, retries a few times if someone does not answer, and can draw a spare route in case one breaks.

sections.title: Worked Example in the Appendix
sections.content:
The appendix uses a topology with nodes R1 to R7 and a controller. A policy at Root R1 has Leaf nodes R2, R6 and R7 and one CP that optimizes the IGP metric.

In the first tree, with non-adjacent Replication segments, R1 replicates to R2, and R2 replicates to R6 and R7. R2 is a Bud node: it is a Leaf and also a transit node. R3, R4 and R5 hold no state for the tree. In SR-MPLS, R2 reaches R6 and R7 by pushing their Node-SIDs ahead of the Tree-SID. In SRv6, the copy to R7 goes through an SR Policy using an End.X function with USD at R4.

In the second tree, the segments are adjacent: R1 to R2, R2 to R3 and R5, R3 to R6 and R5 to R7. Only R4 has no state, and every copy simply carries the same Tree-SID on each link.
sections.eli5: The examples show a small map of seven towns and walk through how a message gets copied and delivered to the chosen ones.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The document has no IANA actions. Its security considerations largely repeat those of RFC 9524. The SR domain must be protected from outside attackers. Without correct MPLS or SRv6 protections at its edge, outsiders could send packets to receivers of multipoint services.

If a controller provisions Replication segments incorrectly, they can form a loop, and replicated packets can create a storm until the MPLS TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit reaches zero. Control plane protocols such as PCEP and BGP can use their own security mechanisms. For SRv6, ICMPv6 Parameter Problem messages (Code 2) could be abused to attack a source node.
sections.eli5: Keep strangers out of the delivery network, and make sure the planner draws a map without circles, or copies will keep running in loops.
